hints: Notice the word uniform - the electric field strength $E$ has the same magnitude and direction at every point along the particle path.
Connect the field to motion using $F = qE$ for the electric force and then $F = ma$ for the acceleration.
Ask yourself what must happen to velocity and displacement if the particle keeps gaining velocity in the direction of a steady force.
walkthrough: The field is uniform, so electric field strength $E$ is constant in magnitude and direction where the particle moves.
The force due to the field is $F = qE$. With constant charge $q$ and constant $E$, the force $F$ is constant and non-zero.
Use Newton's second law $F = ma$, rearranged as $a = F/m = qE/m$. With constant $F$ and constant mass $m$, acceleration $a$ is constant and non-zero.
Constant non-zero acceleration means velocity $v$ changes steadily and displacement $s$ increases at an increasing rate, so neither is constant.
It also means acceleration itself does not change, so rate of change of acceleration is zero.
Therefore only acceleration has a constant non-zero value. This is option A.

options.A: Uniform field gives constant force $F = qE$ and so constant $a = F/m$, which is non-zero because $q$ and $E$ are non-zero.
options.B: Displacement from the start keeps increasing as the particle moves, so it is not constant.
options.C: Because acceleration is constant, its rate of change is zero, not a constant non-zero value.
options.D: A non-zero acceleration means velocity changes continuously, so velocity is not constant.
